questions.prompt: What is the average time complexity of looking up a key in a `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`?
questions.explanation: `Dictionary` is a hash table: it hashes the key with `GetHashCode()` to jump straight to a bucket, so lookups are O(1) on average. Lots of hash collisions (e.g. a bad `GetHashCode`) degrade it towards O(n). `SortedDictionary` is O(log n).

Modifying a `List<T>` while enumerating it invalidates the enumerator. The `Remove` succeeds (count becomes 2), then the next `MoveNext()` notices the list's version changed and throws `InvalidOperationException`. To remove while iterating, use `list.RemoveAll(...)` or loop backwards with a `for`.

questions.prompt: Which built-in collection guarantees unique elements and has O(1) average `Contains`?
questions.explanation: `HashSet<T>` is a hash table of values only: `Add` returns false for duplicates and `Contains` is O(1) on average. `SortedSet<T>` also enforces uniqueness but is a tree, so operations are O(log n). `List<T>.Contains` is O(n).
`Pop` returns the last item pushed: 3. The trick is `new Queue<int>(stack)`: it *enumerates* the stack, and a stack enumerates in pop order (3, 2, 1). So the queue's first item is 3.

questions.prompt: Which built-in collection is last-in, first-out (LIFO)?
questions.explanation: `Stack<T>`: `Push` adds to the top, `Pop` removes the most recently pushed item. `Queue<T>` is first-in, first-out: `Enqueue` at the back, `Dequeue` from the front.

questions.prompt: Which built-in collection is first-in, first-out (FIFO)?
questions.explanation: `Queue<T>` hands items back in the order they were added. `PriorityQueue` dequeues the lowest *priority* first, not the oldest, and `Stack<T>` is LIFO.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of inserting an item at the start of a `List<T>` holding n items?
questions.explanation: `List<T>` is backed by an array, so `Insert(0, x)` shifts every existing element along by one: O(n). Adding at the *end* is amortised O(1). If you need cheap inserts at both ends, use `LinkedList<T>` or a deque-style structure.

questions.prompt: What is the amortised time complexity of `List<T>.Add`?
questions.explanation: When the backing array is full, `Add` allocates one twice the size and copies (O(n)), but doubling makes that rare enough that the average cost per `Add` is O(1). Pass a capacity to the constructor if you know the size up front.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of looking up a key in a `SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue>`?
questions.explanation: `SortedDictionary` is a balanced binary search tree (red-black), so lookups, inserts and removes are O(log n), and it enumerates in key order. `Dictionary` is a hash table: O(1) on average, but no ordering.

questions.prompt: Which interface adds index-based access (`this[int]`, `Insert`, `IndexOf`) on top of `ICollection<T>`?
questions.explanation: The ladder is `IEnumerable<T>` (iterate) → `ICollection<T>` (Count, Add, Remove, Contains) → `IList<T>` (index access). `IReadOnlyCollection<T>` only adds `Count` to `IEnumerable<T>`.

questions.prompt: What does each of `IEnumerable<T>`, `ICollection<T>` and `IList<T>` add over the one before it?
questions.answer: IEnumerable<T>: iterate only. ICollection<T>: adds Count, Add, Remove, Contains, Clear. IList<T>: adds index access (this[i], Insert, IndexOf, RemoveAt).
distractors: IEnumerable<T> adds Count; ICollection<T> adds indexing; IList<T> adds sorting.
They're interchangeable; IList<T> is just the newest name.
IList<T> is read-only; ICollection<T> adds the ability to modify it.
questions.explanation: Accept the least capable interface you need as a parameter (often `IEnumerable<T>` or `IReadOnlyList<T>`) and return the most useful concrete type. Asking for `IList<T>` when you only iterate rules out callers with a plain sequence.

questions.prompt: Can you change the length of an existing array (e.g. an `int[]`) after it's created?
distractors: Only if it was declared with var
questions.explanation: Arrays have a fixed length. `Array.Resize` looks like it resizes, but it allocates a *new* array, copies the elements and updates your variable. Use `List<T>` when the size needs to change.

Setting via the indexer adds *or overwrites*, so Ada becomes 37 with no error. `TryGetValue` returns false for a missing key (no exception), so -1 is printed. `Add` refuses an existing key and throws `ArgumentException`.
